abstract: We consider the equations of linear adiabatic oscillations of stars analytically. There are two known first integrals of nonradial oscillations of spherically symmetric stars, which exist for any stellar structure. One is obtained by integrating the linearized Poisson equation in the case of radial oscillations. The other is derived from momentum conservation in the case of dipolar oscillations. Both of these integrals reduce the order of the differential equations from four to two, which is not trivial. We find that this property can be understood from the fact that the problem of adiabatic stellar oscillations can be formulated as a Hamiltonian system. We then examine the symmetry of the system that corresponds to these first integrals. We finally show that there is no other first integral that is valid for arbitrary structures of stars.

articleTitle: Sunspot Gyroresonance Emission at 17 GHz: A Statistical Study
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We investigate the sunspot gyroresonance emission at 17 GHz using the synoptic database of the Nobeyama Radioheliograph. Our statistical study is based on full disk observations obtained during the maximum of Cycle 22 (1992–94). We study the center-to-limb variation of the brightness and polarization of the sunspot radio emission and present some cases of polarization reversal. We find that the radio emission is most likely 3rd-harmonic gyroresonance emission arising from 2000 G fields in transition region, or low corona temperatures.

articleTitle: The Parsec-Scale Jet of PKS 0637−752
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Chandra observations of the quasar PKS 0637-752 during its checkout phase resulted in the unexpected detection of a luminous kiloparsec-scale X-ray jet. The apparent superluminal speed of this jet on the parsec-scale, based on two VSOP and four ground-based observations, has proven crucial to understanding the X-ray production in the arcsec-scale jet. We present here for the first time the full details of the ground-based observations used to determine the parsec-scale jet speed, describe the results of a third VSOP observation, and examine the reported jet speed in the light of more recent ground-based VLBI observations. We find some evidence of increased source activity coincident with extrapolated epochs of jet component ejection, although the monitoring of the source is relatively sparse and the ejection epochs are not tightly constrained. We also construct the spectral energy distribution for the nucleus of PKS 0637-752 and show that it can be modelled well in terms of a one-zone synchrotron self-Compton model of an electron-positron jet with a Doppler factor of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 10$</tex>, consistent with the results of the VLBI observations.

articleTitle: Observations of Prominence Eruptions with Two Radioheliographs, SSRT, and NoRH
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We address simultaneous observations of eruptive prominences with two radioheliographs, SSRT at 5.7 GHz and NoRH at 17 and 34 GHz. Three events are presented: 1997 September 27, 2000 September 4, and 2001 January 14. We analyze them using images observed in microwaves, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{H}\alpha$</tex>, images from Extreme ultraviolet Imaging Telescope on board Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOHO), and white-light images from Large Angle and Spectrometric Coronagraph (SOHO/LASCO). We address three stages of the eruptive process: 1) pre-eruptive ascent, 2) rapid acceleration, 3) free expansion, and the overall kinematics of the ejecta. We estimate the densities and kinetic temperatures of prominences, and also the velocities and accelerations of ejecta. The main body of a prominence is surrounded by low-density cool extensions mixed with the coronal plasma, but the transition from the cool prominence to the hot plasma is sharp. From microwave and LASCO observations with overlapping fields of view we identify a radio prominence and a core of a coronal mass ejection (CME). Their temperature remains at about 5000 K, while the brightenings observed in extreme ultraviolet are probably due to only skin-heating. We discuss the observations in terms of our Dual-Filament CME initiation model.

articleTitle: Common Correlations between 60, 100, and 140$\, {\mu \mathrm {m}}$ Intensities in the Galactic Plane and Magellanic Clouds
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We investigated the far-infrared SED of the Galaxy and the Magellanic Clouds by using the COBE (COsmic Background Explorer)/DIRBE (Diffuse InfraRed Background Experiment) ZSMA (Zodi-Subtracted Mission Average) maps at wavelengths of 60<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\, {\mu \mathrm {m}}$</tex>, 100<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\, {\mu \mathrm {m}}$</tex>, and 140<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\, {\mu \mathrm {m}}$</tex>. We analyzed three regions: the galactic plane region with the galactic latitude <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\vert b\vert < 5^{\circ}$</tex>, the Large Magellanic Cloud region, and the Small Magellanic Cloud region. Because the dust optical depth is much smaller in the far-infrared than in the visible, we could observe cumulative far-infrared radiation from regions with various interstellar radiation field in the line of sight. As a consequence of considering such an effect, we found a common far-infrared color correlation between the 140–100<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\, {\mu \mathrm {m}}$</tex> and 100–60<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\, {\mu \mathrm {m}}$</tex> intensity ratios in all three galaxies. Although this color correlation cannot be explained by any existing model, it fits very well the far-infrared color of nearby star-forming galaxies.

articleTitle: A Study of Accelerated Electrons in Solar Flares Using Microwave and X-Ray Observations
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We consider manifestations of accelerated electrons in microwave and hard X-ray emissions from solar flares. To meet our objectives, we discuss two events — those of 1999 March 16 and February 16. The first event is a short-duration burst, while the second is a long-duration event. An analysis of the first event leads to the conclusion that: 1) a seemingly single-loop configuration can actually be a double-loop one, and 2) it is possible that the pitch-angle distribution of the radio-emitting electrons can be anisotropic with practically no non-zero pitch angles. The second event shows seemingly intersecting flaring loops, and the formation of a post-eruptive arcade that can proceed as a series of double-loop interactions. From these and other published results, we conclude that: 1) double-loop configurations can be responsible for flares showing diverse morphologies and time profiles; 2) the pitch-angle distribution of accelerated electrons can be strongly anisotropic, with an excess of small angles, contributing to a rather narrow energy range of the microwave-emitting electrons.

articleTitle: Time Delays for the Giant Quadruple Lensed Quasar SDSS J1004+4112: Prospects for Determining the Density Profile of the Lensing Cluster
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We investigated the dependence of the time delays for the large-separation gravitationally lensed quasar SDSS J1004+4112 on the inner mass profile of the lensing cluster. Adopting a mass model whose innermost density profile was parameterized as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rho \propto r^{-\alpha}$</tex>, we derived a series of mass models that can fit the observational data, and then compute the probability distribution functions of time delays. We find that larger <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> has longer time delays, longer tails at the higher end of the probability distribution, and larger model uncertainties. The ratios of the time delays slightly depend on the slope, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex>. Among others, time delays between images C and A (or B) have little dependence on the inner slope, particularly when the time delays are short. The dependence of time delays on <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> is well fitted by a linear form, which reflects the well-known degeneracy between the mass profile and time delays. We performed a Monte Carlo simulation to illustrate how well the inner slope can be constrained from measurements of time delays. We found that measurements of more than one time delay resulted in reasonably tight constraints on the inner slope (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sigma_{\alpha} \lesssim 0.25$</tex>), while only one time delay could not determine the inner slope very well. Our result indicates that time delays indeed serve as a powerful tool to determine the mass profile, despite the complexity of the lensing cluster.

articleTitle: SiO Maser Survey of the Inner Bar of the Galactic Bulge
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We surveyed 291 MSX/2 MASS infrared objects in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$7^{\circ} \!\times 2^{\circ}$</tex> area of the galactic center in the 43 GHz SiO <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J = 1 \hbox{--} 0 v=1$</tex> and 2 maser lines, obtaining accurate radial velocities of 163 detected objects. The surveyed area is the region where the IRAS catalog is incomplete due to contamination by high source density. The objects in the present MSX/2 MASS sample were chosen to have similar infrared characteristics to those of the previous SiO-maser-survey samples based on the color-selected IRAS sources. The sampling based on the 2 MASS catalog causes a bias to the foreside objects of the bulge due to heavy obscuration by interstellar dust; the detections considerably leaned on the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$V_{\mathrm{lsr}}<0$</tex> side. The <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$l \hbox{--} V$</tex> diagram reveals two conspicuous features, which were not present or tenuous in the previous studies: one feature indicating a linear velocity increase with longitude with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\vert l\vert < {1\rlap {.}{}^{\mathrm {\circ }}5}$</tex>, which is likely to be associated with the inner bar, and the other feature having considerably eccentric velocities, more than those of the normal <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$x_1$</tex>-orbit family feature. The extinction-corrected <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K$</tex> magnitudes (if used as a distance modulus) tend to show a sequential deposition of these objects along the line of sight toward the galactic center, depending on their radial velocities. The tendency that appeared in the distance measures is consistent with the bulge–bar dynamical model utilizing the periodic orbit families in the bar potential.

articleTitle: λ Bootis-Like Abundances in the Vega-Like, γ Doradus Type-Pulsator HD 218396
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The elemental abundances of 16 elements in the Vega-like and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex> Doradus-type variable star HD 218396 have been determined. A model atmosphere with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\mathrm{eff}} = 7250 \,\mathrm{K}, \log g = 4.30$</tex>, and a metallicity of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$[\mathrm{M/H}] =-0.50$</tex> was used. A moderate, but definite, deficiency in the abundance of iron, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$[\mathrm{Fe/H}] =-0.55 \pm 0.1$</tex>, has been confirmed. Other elements, Na through Ba, are also as under-abundant as Fe. On the other hand, two light elements, C and O, show solar abundances. These findings confirm the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda$</tex> Bootis nature of this star, which had been so classified based on a low-resolution optical spectrum. The observed abundance pattern provides a constraint in understanding the nature of this interesting object, which shows excess emission in the infrared region, implying that the star is accompanied by a dusty-debris disk, and at the same time shows photometric and spectroscopic variations arising from non-radial high-order g-mode pulsations.

articleTitle: High-Resolution Studies of the Dense Molecular Cores toward Massive Star-Forming Regions
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present the results of the imaging of dense molecular cores in three massive star-forming regions (IRAS 02461+6147, IRAS 03035+5819, and IRAS 06058+2138), which are associated with luminous infrared sources with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1 \hbox{--} 5 \times 10^{4} \,{{{L}_{\odot}}}$</tex>. The C<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${{18\atop} \mathrm{O}}$</tex> (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J = 1 \hbox{--} 0$</tex>) molecular emission from the dense cores and the thermal dust and/or free-free emission at 98 GHz and 110 GHz in the hot core candidates have been imaged with a resolution of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim {4{}^{\mathrm {\prime \prime }}}$</tex> using the Nobeyama Millimeter Array. We identified 28 C<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${{18\atop} \mathrm{O}}$</tex> dense cores, whose mass, effective radius, and line-width range from 2.1 to 29<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${M}_{\odot}$</tex>, from 0.013 to 0.108 pc, and from 0.7 to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2.7 \,\mathrm{km} \,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$</tex>, respectively, and identified four thermal dust millimeter continuum sources (MCSs). We divided the C<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${{18\atop} \mathrm{O}}$</tex> cores into two types, a turbulent core and a non-turbulent core. The non-turbulent cores are similar to the typical cores in the low-mass star-forming regions. The turbulent cores have a higher average <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{H}_2$</tex> density than those of the non-turbulent cores, and the external pressure of these cores is 100–1000 times higher than that of low-mass star-forming regions. Three of the turbulent cores are associated with massive protostar candidates and the intensity peak of MCS. Massive stars are formed from the turbulent cores which are gravitationally bound. In order to form such a turbulent core a molecular cloud has a large kinetic motion and a large mass.

articleTitle: Energy Conversion Efficiency in Prompt Emissions of Gamma-Ray Bursts
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Using 52 gamma-ray bursts observed and localized by BeppoSAX and HETE-2, a comprehensive analysis of the correlation between the properties of prompt emissions and the brightness of the afterglows was performed. We found a highly significant correlation between the isotropic total energy of prompt emission and luminosity of optical afterglow. There is also a correlation between the fluence in prompt emission and the magnitude of the optical afterglow. We then investigated the energy conversion efficiency in prompt emissions of gamma-ray bursts using 24 bursts with the known redshift. We calculated the kinetic energy of relativistic shells from the luminosities of the optical afterglows. The energy-conversion efficiency, as estimated by comparing this kinetic energy with the total radiated energy of prompt emission, is distributed between about 1% and 40%. This result suggests that the ratio of the Lorentz factor of two colliding shells is large, or the fraction of shock energy that goes into the electrons is small for the internal shock scenario.

articleTitle: Discovery of a λ Bootis Like Abundance Pattern in the Pulsating Algol-Type System RZ Cassiopeiae
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The abundances of eight elements (C through Fe) were determined in the primary star of the short-period Algol-type binary RZ Cas relative to the A3 V spectroscopic standard star <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> PsA. Definite under-abundances (by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-0.45 \,\mathrm{dex}$</tex> or more) of Mg, Si, Ti, Cr, and Fe were established. On the other hand, light elements C and O show solar abundances, and Ca is slightly under-abundant (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim-0.3 \,\mathrm{dex}$</tex>). This abundance pattern demonstrates that RZ Cas shows a characteristic of mild <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda$</tex> Boo-type stars. This finding raises a question on the physical relations between the metallicity (abundance anomaly), the pulsational characteristics, and the mass accretion processes.

articleTitle: Strong Emission-Line Galaxies at Low Redshifts in the Field around the Quasar SDSSp J104433.04−012502.2
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We discuss the observational properties of strong emission-line galaxies at low redshifts found by our deep imaging survey for high-redshift Ly<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> emitters. In our survey, we used a narrow-band filter, NB816 (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda_{\mathrm{center}} = 8150 \,{\AA}$</tex> with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mbox{FWHM} = 120 \,\mbox{\AA}$</tex> FWHM<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$= 120 \,{\AA}$</tex>), and an intermediate-band filter, IA827 (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda_{\mathrm{center}} = 8270 \,{\AA}$</tex> with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mbox{FWHM} = 340 \,\mbox{\AA}$</tex> FWHM<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$= 340 \,{\AA}$</tex>). In this survey, 62 NB816-excess (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$> 0.9 \,\mathrm{mag} > 0.9 \,\mathrm{mag}$</tex>) and 21 IA827-excess (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$> 0.8 \,\mathrm{mag} > 0.8 \,\mathrm{mag}$</tex>) objects were found. Among them, we found 20 NB816-excess and 4 IA827-excess Ly<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> emitter candidates. Therefore, it turns out that 42 NB816-excess and 17 IA827-excess objects are strong emission-line objects at lower redshifts. Since 4 objects in the two low-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z$</tex> samples are common, the total number of strong low-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z$</tex> emitters is 55. Applying our photometric redshift technique, we identified 7 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{H}\alpha$</tex> emitters at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z \approx 0.24$</tex>, 20 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{H}\beta$</tex>–[O III] ones at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z \approx 0.65$</tex>, and 11 [O II] ones at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z \approx 1.19$</tex>. However, we could not determine reliable photometric redshifts of the remaining 17 emitters. The distributions of their rest frame equivalent widths are consistently understood based on recent studies of galaxy evolution from <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z \sim 1$</tex> to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z \sim 0$</tex>.

articleTitle: Lyα Emitters at z = 5.7 in the Subaru Deep Field
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present the properties of Ly<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> emitters (LAEs) at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z=5.7$</tex> in the Subaru Deep Field. A photometric sample of 89 LAE candidates was constructed from narrow-band data down to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathit{NB816} = 26.0$</tex> (AB) in a continuous <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$725 \,\mathrm{arcmin}^2$</tex> area. Spectra of 39 objects satisfying the photometric selection criteria for LAEs were obtained with Subaru and Keck II Telescopes, among which 28 were confirmed LAEs, one was a nearby galaxy, and eight were unclassified. We also obtained spectra of another 24 NB816-excess objects in the field, identifying six additional LAEs. We find that the Ly<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> luminosity function derived from the photometric sample is reproduced well by a Schechter function with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L^\star = 7.9^{+3.0}_{-2.2} \times 10^{42} \,\mathrm{erg} \,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\phi^\star = 6.3^{+3.0}_{-2.0} \times 10^{-4} \,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-3}$</tex> for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha =-1.5$</tex> (fixed) over the whole luminosity range of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L \simeq 3 \times 10^{42} \hbox{--} 3 \times 10^{43} \,\mathrm{erg} \,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$</tex>. We then measured the rest-frame Ly<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> equivalent widths for the confirmed LAEs, to find that the median among the 28 objects satisfying the photometric selection criteria is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$W_{0}^{\mathrm{i}} = 233 \,{\AA}$</tex>. We infer that 30%-40% of LAEs at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z=5.7$</tex> exceed <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$W_{0}^{\mathrm{i}} = 240 \,{\AA}$</tex>. These large-EW objects probably cannot be accounted for by ordinary star-forming populations with a Salpeter IMF. We also find that LAEs with fainter far-UV luminosities have larger EWs. Finally, we derived the far-UV luminosity function of LAEs down to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\mathrm{UV}} \simeq-19.6$</tex> using the photometric sample, and compared it with that of Lyman-break galaxies (LBGs). We find that as high as about 80% of LBGs at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z \sim 6$</tex> have <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$W_{0}^{\mathrm{i}} \ge 100 \,{\AA}$</tex>, in sharp contrast to lower-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z$</tex> counterparts.

articleTitle: Chemical Abundances in the Secondary Star of the Black Hole Binary V4641 Sagittarii (SAX J1819.3−2525)
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on detailed spectroscopic studies performed for the secondary star in the black hole binary (micro-quasar) V4641 Sgr in order to examine its surface chemical composition and to see if its surface shows any signature of pollution by ejecta from a supernova explosion. High-resolution spectra of V4641 Sgr observed in the quiescent state in the blue-visual region are compared with those of the two bright well-studied B9 stars (14 Cyg and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\nu$</tex> Cap) observed with the same instrument. The effective temperature of V4641 Sgr (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$10500 \pm 200 \,\mathrm{K}$</tex>) is estimated from the strengths of He I lines, while its rotational velocity, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$v \sin i$</tex> (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$95 \pm 10 \,\mathrm{km} \,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$</tex>), is estimated from the profile of the Mg II line at 4481 Å. We obtain abundances of 10 elements and find definite over-abundances of N (by 0.8 dex or more) and Na (by 0.8 dex) in V4641 Sgr. From line-by-line comparisons of eight other elements (C, O, Mg, Al, Si, Ti, Cr, and Fe) between V4641 Sgr and the two reference stars, we conclude that there is no apparent difference in the abundances of these elements between V4641 Sgr and the two normal late B-type stars, which have been reported to have solar abundances. An evolutionary model of a massive close binary system has been constructed to explain the abundances observed in V4641 Sgr. The model suggests that the progenitor of the black hole forming supernova was as massive as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 35 \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex> on the main-sequence and, after becoming a <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 10 \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex> He star, underwent a “dark” explosion which ejected only N–and Na-rich outer layer of the He star without radioactive <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${{56\atop} \mathrm{Ni}}$</tex>.

articleTitle: Three-Dimensional Distribution of the ISM in the Milky Way Galaxy: II. The Molecular Gas Disk
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We created a three-dimensional distribution map of molecular gas throughout the Milky Way galaxy using the latest <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${{12\atop} \mathrm{CO}}$</tex> (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J = 1 \hbox{--} 0$</tex>) survey data cube and the rotation curve based on the kinematic distance. The radial distribution of the molecular gas shows a central peak and a second peak around <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$0.5 \,R_0$</tex> (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R_0$</tex>: the solar Galactocentric distance). The thickness of the molecular disk slightly increases from 48 pc to 160 pc with the Galactocentric distance within a radius range of 0–11 kpc. We were able to trace the Outer, the Perseus, the Sagittarius–Carina, the Scutum–Crux, and the Norma arms as logarithmic spiral arms with pitch angles of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$11 {{}^{\circ }} \hbox{--} 15^\circ$</tex>. Considering that the pitch angles of the spiral arms are within this range, the Norma and the Outer arms seem to be identified as the same spiral arm. We could also trace a midplane displacement, whose amplitude is nearly constant inside a 10 kpc radius and increases beyond this radius. The ridges of the midplane displacement form the leading spiral arms.

articleTitle: The 2003/2004 Superoutburst of SDSS J013701.06−091234.9
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on time-resolved photometry of the superoutburst of an SU UMa-type dwarf nova, SDSS J013701.06-091234.9, in 2003 December–2004 January. The obtained light curves definitely show superhumps with a period of 0.056686(12)d, which is one of the shortest superhump periods among those of SU UMa-type dwarf novae ever observed. Considering quiescent photometric studies, we estimated the fractional superhump excess to be 0.024. Spectroscopic observations by Szkody et al. (2003, AJ, 126, 1499) provided evidence for TiO bands despite the short orbital period, implying that the system has a luminous secondary star. We have drawn a color-color diagram of SU UMa-type dwarf novae in quiescence using 2MASS archives, revealing that the location of this star in the color-color diagram deviates from the general trend. The distance to the system was roughly estimated to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$300 \pm 80 \,\mathrm{pc}$</tex>, using the empirical period–absolute magnitude relation and based on the proper motion.

articleTitle: An Extrasolar Planet Transit Search with Subaru Suprime-Cam
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report the results of a prototype photometric search for transiting extrasolar planets using Subaru Suprime-Cam. Out of about 100000 stars monitored around the Galactic plane (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$l=90^{\circ}, b=0^{\circ}$</tex>), we find that 7700 show photometric precision better than 1% for 60s exposures, which is required to detect extrasolar planets by the transit method. Thus, Suprime-Cam has the photometric stability and accuracy necessary for a transiting planet survey. During this observing run, we detected three objects (around 18.5 mag for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$i'$</tex>-band) that exhibit a single full transit-like light curve with a fractional depth of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$< 5\%$</tex>. While a spectroscopic follow-up remains to be done using future telescopes in the 20–30 m class, the estimated parameters for the three systems are consistent with the planetary size companions around main-sequence stars. We also found two eclipsing binary candidates and eleven variable stars exhibiting W UMa-like light curves.

articleTitle: Do Ultraluminous X-Ray Sources Really Contain Intermediate-Mass Black Holes?
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: An open question remains whether Ultraluminous X-ray Sources (ULXs) really contain intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs). We carefully investigated the XMM-Newton EPIC spectra of four ULXs that were claimed to be strong candidates of IMBHs by several authors. We first tried fitting by the standard spectral model of disk blackbody (DBB) <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${+}$</tex> power-law (PL), finding good fits to all of the data, in agreement with others. We, however, found that the PL component dominates the DBB component at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 0.3$</tex> to 10keV. Thus, the black hole parameters derived solely from the minor DBB component are questionable. Next, we tried to fit the same data by the “<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$p$</tex>-free disk model” without the PL component, assuming an effective temperature profile of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\mathrm{eff}} \propto r^{-p}$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r$</tex> is the disk radius. Interestingly, in spite of one less free-model parameter, we obtained similarly good fits with much higher innermost disk temperatures, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1.8 < kT_{\mathrm{in}} < 3.2 \,\mathrm{keV}$</tex>. More importantly, we obtained <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$p \sim 0.5$</tex>, just the value predicted by the slim (super-critical) disk theory, rather than <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$p = 0.75$</tex> that is expected from the standard disk model. The estimated black hole masses from the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$p$</tex>-free disk model are much smaller; <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M \lesssim 40 \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex>. Furthermore, we applied a more sophisticated slim-disk model by Kawaguchi (2003, ApJ, 593, 69), and obtained good fits with roughly consistent black hole masses. We thus conclude that the central engines of these ULXs are super-critical accretion flows to stellar-mass black holes.

Author Keywords: X-rays: individual (NGC 5204 X-1, NGC 4559 X-7, NGC 4559 X-10, NGC 1313 X-2)

articleTitle: Formation of Magnetically Supported Disks during Hard-to-Soft Transitions in Black Hole Accretion Flows
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We carried out three-dimensional global resistive magnetohydrodynamic simulations of the cooling instability in optically thin hot black hole accretion flows by assuming bremsstrahlung cooling. General relativistic effects are simulated using the pseudo-Newtonian potential. The cooling instability grows when the density of the accretion disk becomes sufficiently large. We found that as the instability grows the accretion flow changes from an optically thin, hot, gas pressure-supported state (low/hard state) to a cooler, magnetically supported, quasi-steady state. During this transition, the magnetic pressure exceeds the gas pressure because the disk shrinks in the vertical direction while almost conserving the toroidal magnetic flux. Since further vertical contraction of the disk is suppressed by magnetic pressure, the cool disk stays in an optically thin, spectrally hard state. The magnetically supported disk exists for a time scale much longer than the thermal time scale, and comparable to the accretion time scale. We examined the stability of the magnetically supported disk analytically, assuming that the toroidal magnetic flux is conserved, and found it to be thermally and secularly stable. Our findings may explain why black hole candidates stay in luminous, hard state even when their luminosity exceeds the threshold for the onset of the cooling instability.

articleTitle: Horizontal and Vertical Flow Structure in Emerging Flux Regions
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: In order to obtain an overall view of the flow structure of convective gas in emerging flux regions (EFRs), we studied three EFRs in two solar active regions, NOAA 8218 and NOAA 10774. Using the Local Correlation Tracking method, we found several horizontally divergent flow structures, which were stable over a period of 1 hour, in 2 EFRs in NOAA 8218. The horizontal flow velocities and the sizes of the structures were around <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$500 \,\mathrm{m} \,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$</tex> and about 4 mm in radius, respectively. We analyzed another dataset of NOAA 10774 using spectroscopic methods and found temporarily stable up-ward gas flows in the central part of the EFR. The line-of-sight velocities were around <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$150 \,\mathrm{m} \,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$</tex> and the size of the flow patch was 2 to 5 mm in radius. These results support our previous findings that convective-cell-like flow appears in the central part of an EFR. We estimated from these results that the depth of the flow cell in EFRs is about 600 Km, and the turn-over time of the cell is about 2 hours.

articleTitle: Analysis of Adiabatic Dipolar Oscillations of Stars
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We theoretically discuss adiabatic dipolar oscillations of stars, fully taking into account the variation in the gravitational field. By suitably choosing the dependent variables, and using the first integral specific to dipolar oscillations, we derive the second-order system of ordinary differential equations, which is the same in form as that obtained by neglecting the Eulerian perturbation to the gravitational potential. The derived system suggests that the conventional expressions of the critical frequencies should be corrected. In addition, we present a rigorous scheme to classify the dipolar eigenmodes of linear adiabatic oscillations of spherically symmetric stars.

articleTitle: Soft X-Ray Transmission Spectroscopy of a Warm/Hot Intergalactic Medium with XEUS
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We discuss the detectability of a Warm/Hot Intergalactic Medium (WHIM) via absorption lines toward bright point sources with a future X-ray satellite mission, XEUS. While we consider bright QSOs as specific examples, the methodology can be applied to bright gamma-ray burst afterglows. We created mock absorption spectra for bright QSOs (more than 20 QSOs over all sky) using the light-cone output of a cosmological hydrodynamic simulation. We assumed that the WHIM is under collisional and photo-ionization equilibrium. If WHIM has a constant metallicity of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$Z = 0.1 \,Z_{ {\odot }}$</tex>, approximately 2 O VII absorption line systems with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ > 3 \,\sigma > 3 \,\sigma$</tex> will be detected on average along a random line-of-sight toward bright QSOs up to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z=0.3$</tex> for a 30 ks exposure.

articleTitle: Chandra and XMM-Newton Observations of a Group of Galaxies, HCG 62
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present results from Chandra and XMM-Newton observations of a bright group of galaxies, HCG 62. There are two cavities at about <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$30{}^{\prime\prime}$</tex> northeast and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$20{}^{\prime\prime}$</tex> southwest of the central galaxy in the Chandra image. The energy spectrum shows no significant change in the cavity compared with that in the surrounding region. The radial X-ray profile is described by the sum of the 3-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta$</tex> components with core radii of about 2, 10, and 160 kpc. We studied the radial distributions of the temperature and the metal abundance with a joint spectral fit for both data; two temperatures were required in the inner <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r< 2'$</tex> (36 kpc) region. A sharp drop of the temperature at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r \sim 5'$</tex> implies a gravitational mass density even lower than the gas density, suggesting that the gas may not be in hydrostatic equilibrium. The Fe and Si abundances are 1–2 solar at the center, and drop to about 0.1 solar at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r \sim 10'$</tex>. The O abundance is less than 0.5 solar, and shows a flatter profile. The observed metal distribution supports the view that iron and silicon are produced by type Ia supernova (SN Ia) in the central galaxy, while galactic winds by SN II have caused a wide distribution of oxygen. The supporting mechanism of the cavity is discussed. The pressure for the sum of electrons and the magnetic field is too low to displace the hot group gas, and the required pressure due to high-energy protons is nearly 700-times higher than the electron pressure. This leaves the origin of the cavities a puzzle; we also discuss other possible origins of the cavities.

articleTitle: Detailed XMM-Newton Observation of the Cluster of Galaxies Abell 1060
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present results from an XMM-Newton observation of the non-cooling flow cluster Abell 1060. The large effective area of XMM-Newton enabled us to investigate the nature of this cluster in unprecedented detail. From the observed surface brightness distribution, we found that the gravitational mass distribution is well described by the Navarro–Frenk–White (1997, ApJ, 490, 493) profile, but with a central density slope of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 1.5$</tex>. We undoubtedly detected a radial temperature decrease of as large as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 30\%$</tex> from the center to the outer region (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r \sim 13'$</tex>), which seems to be much larger than that expected from the temperature profile averaged over nearby clusters. We established that the temperature of a region <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 7'$</tex> southeast of the center is higher than the azimuthally averaged temperature of the same radius by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 20\%$</tex>. Since the pressure of this region already reaches equilibrium with the environment, the temperature structure can be interpreted as having been produced between <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$4 \times 10^{7} \,\mathrm{yr}$</tex> (the sound-crossing time) and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$3 \times 10^{8} \,\mathrm{yr}$</tex> (the thermal conduction time) ago. We found that a high-metallicity blob located at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim {1\rlap {.}{}^{\mathrm {\prime }}5}$</tex> northeast of NGC 3311 is more extended, and its iron mass of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1.9 \times 10^{7} \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex> is larger by an order of magnitude than that estimated from our Chandra observation. The amount of iron can still be considered as being injected solely from the elliptical galaxy NGC 3311.

articleTitle: Bigradient Phase Referencing
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We propose bigradient phase referencing (BPR), a new radio-observation technique, and report on its performance using the Japanese very-long-baseline-interferometry network (JVN). In this method, a weak source is detected by phase-referencing using a primary calibrator, in order to play a role as a secondary calibrator for phase-referencing to a weak target. We will be given the opportunity to select a calibrator from lots of milli-Jansky sources, one of which may be located at a position closer to the target. With such a smaller separation, high-quality phase-referencing can be achieved. A subsequent more-sophisticated calibration can relocate the array’s focus to a hypothetical point much closer to the target; a higher quality of phase referencing is available. Our demonstrative observations with strong radio sources have proved the capabilities of the BPR in terms of the image dynamic ranges and astrometric reproducibility. The image dynamic range on a target has been improved by a factor of about six compared to that of normal phase-referencing; the resultant position difference of the target’s emission between two epochs was only <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$62 \pm 50$</tex> microarcsecond, even with less than 2300-km baselines at 8.4 GHz and fast-switching between a target-calibrator pair separated by a <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${2\rlap {.}{}^{\mathrm {\circ }}1}$</tex>.

articleTitle: An Optically Dark GRB Observed by HETE-2: GRB 051022
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: GRB 051022 was detected at 13:07:58 on 2005 October 22 UT by HETE-2. The location of GRB 051022 was determined immediately by the flight localization system. This burst contained multiple pulses, and had a rather long duration of about 190 s. The detections of candidate X-ray and radio afterglows were reported, whereas no optical afterglow was found. Optical spectroscopic observations of the host galaxy revealed a redshift of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z = 0.8$</tex>. Using data derived by a HETE-2 observation of the prompt emission, we found absorption of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N_{\mathrm{H}} = (8.8_{-2.9}^{+3.1}) \times 10^{22} \,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$</tex> and visual extinction of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$A_{V} = 49_{-16}^{+17}$</tex> mag in the host galaxy. If this is the case, no detection of any optical transient would be quite reasonable. The absorption derived by Swift XRT observations of the afterglow is fully consistent with those obtained from an early HETE-2 observation of the prompt emission. Our analysis implies an interpretation that the absorbing medium may be outside the external shock at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R \sim 10^{16} \,\mathrm{cm}$</tex>, which could be a dusty molecular cloud.

articleTitle: Milliarcsecond-Scale Structure in the Gamma-Ray Loud Quasar PKS 1622−297
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We made a high-resolution VLBI observation of the gamma-ray loud quasar PKS 1622-297 with the HALCA spacecraft and ground radio telescopes at 5 GHz in 1998 February, almost 3 yr after the source exhibited a spectacular GeV gamma-ray flare. The source shows an elongated structure toward the west on the parsec scale. The visibility data are well modeled by three distinct components: a bright core and two weaker jet components. Comparison with previous observations confirms that the jet components have an apparent superluminal motion up to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$12.1 \,h^{-1} \, c$</tex>, with the inner jet components having lower superluminal speeds. We applied the inverse Compton catastrophe model and derived a Doppler factor, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\delta$</tex>, of 2.45, which is rather lower than those of other gamma-ray loud active galactic nuclei (AGNs), suggesting that the source was in a more quiescent phase at the epoch of our observation. As an alternative probe of the subparsec-scale structure, we also present the results from multiepoch ATCA total flux monitoring, which indicate the presence of persistent intraday variability consistent with refractive interstellar scintillation. We examined the gamma-ray emission mechanism in light of these observations.

articleTitle: Implications for Cosmic Reionization from the Optical Afterglow Spectrum of the Gamma-Ray Burst 050904 at z = 6.3
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The gamma-ray burst (GRB) 050904 at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z = 6.3$</tex> provides the first opportunity to probe the intergalactic medium (IGM) by GRBs at the epoch of reionization. Here, we present a spectral modeling analysis of the optical afterglow spectrum taken by the Subaru Telescope, aiming to constrain the reionization history. The spectrum shows a clear damping wing at wavelengths redward of the Lyman break, and the wing shape can be fitted either by a damped Ly<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> system with a column density of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\log [N_{\mathrm{H {I}}} \,(\mathrm{cm}^{-2})] \sim 21.6$</tex> at a redshift close to the detected metal absorption lines (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z_{\mathrm{metal}} = 6.295$</tex>), or by almost neutral IGM extending to a slightly higher redshift of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z_{\mathrm{IGM,u}} \sim 6.36$</tex>. In the latter case, the difference between the two redshifts may be explained by the acceleration of metal absorbing shells in the activities of the GRB or its progenitor. However, we exclude this possibility by using the light transmission feature around the Ly<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta$</tex> resonance, leading to a firm upper limit of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z_{\mathrm{IGM,u}} \leq 6.314$</tex>. We then show evidence that the IGM was already largely ionized at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z = 6.3$</tex> with the best-fit neutral fraction of IGM, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$x_{\mathrm{H {I}}} \; (\equiv n_{\mathrm{H {I}}} / n_{\mathrm{H}}) = 0.00$</tex>, and upper limits of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$x_{\mathrm{H {I}}} < 0.17$</tex> and 0.60 at 68% and 95% confidence levels, respectively. This is the first direct and quantitative upper limit on <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$x_{\mathrm{H {I}}}$</tex> at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z > 6$</tex>. Various systematic uncertainties are examined, but none of them appears large enough to change our conclusion. To get further information on the reionization, it is important to increase the sample size of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z >rsim 6$</tex> GRBs, in order to find GRBs with low column densities (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\log N_{\mathrm{H {I}}} \lesssim 20$</tex>) within their host galaxies and to make statistical studies of Ly<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> line emission from host galaxies.

articleTitle: Overdensity of X-Ray Sources in the Field of Two Nearby Clusters of Galaxies: XMM-Newton View of A 194 and A 1060
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Two nearby clusters of galaxies, A194 (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z = 0.018$</tex>) and A1060 (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z = 0.0114$</tex>), have been analyzed for their X-ray point-source properties with XMM-Newton EPIC-PN data. A multi-band source detection technique was applied to both of the clusters, resulting in 46 sources from the A194 field and 32 sources from the A1060 field, respectively. The cumulative <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\log (N) \hbox{--} \log(S)$</tex> for a flux limit of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$F_{\mathrm{X}} \geq 1 \times 10^{-14} \,\mathrm{erg} \,\mathrm{cm}^{-2} \,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$</tex> was calculated and compared with that of the Lockman Hole. A <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 3\,\sigma$</tex> excess of X-ray sources was found for the cluster regions. Considering the higher fraction observed in optical studies from the clusters, we estimate that the cluster source density is 6-times higher than the blank-field source density, and 15-times higher than the local group. Our X-ray selected sources have luminosity values of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$10^{39.6} \leq L_{\mathrm{X}} \leq 10^{41.4} \,\mathrm{erg} \,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$</tex>, in which X-ray emission from LMXBs, hot halos and starburst galaxies becomes noticeable. The significance of the source-density excess gradually vanishes for sources with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\mathrm{X}} \geq 10^{40.5} \,\mathrm{erg} \,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$</tex>, at which point the source density becomes comparable to that of the blank-field level. Considering this confined low-luminosity range and the X-ray to optical luminosity ratios (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\mathrm{X}} / L_{\mathrm{B}}$</tex>), the observed overdensity is ascribed to AGN fueling by its infall into cluster environment for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\mathrm{X}} \leq 10^{40.5} \,\mathrm{erg} \,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$</tex> in the X-ray luminosity function. However, the quenching of AGN activity by the deep cluster potential explains why the excess of the source density vanishes for brighter sources.

articleTitle: Milliarcsecond-Scale Spectral Properties and Jet Motions in M 87
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have combined high resolution VLBI Space Observatory Programme (VSOP) data at 1.6 and 4.8 GHz with Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) data at higher frequencies and with similar resolutions to study the spectral properties of the core of M 87 with milliarcsec resolution. The VSOP data allows a more accurate measurement of the turnover frequency, and hence more reliable determination of associated physical parameters of the source. Comparison of the images with previously published images yields no evidence for significant motions of components in the parsec-scale jet. In addition, the brightness temperatures obtained from modelfits to the core are well below the inverse Compton limit, suggesting that the radio emission we are observing is not strongly Doppler boosted.

articleTitle: Plasma Parameters in a Post-Eruptive Arcade Observed with CORONAS-F/SPIRIT, Yohkoh/SXT, SOHO/EIT, and in Microwaves
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The SPectroheliographIc X-Ray Imaging Telescope (SPIRIT) aboard the CORONAS-F spacecraft sometimes observes in the Mg XII 8.42 Å line (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_\mathrm{max} \sim 9 \,\mathrm{MK}$</tex>) large, bright features existing for many hours high in the corona. This fact suggests that plasma beta there might not be small. We identify such a feature observed on 2001 October 22 at a height of 100 Mm with a hot part of a post-eruptive arcade. Using multi-spectral data and radio astronomy methods, we estimate the plasma parameters in the arcade and reveal the coronal magnetic configuration. Several hours after the eruption, the temperature in the arcade was 6–8 MK, and the plasma density was <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(5 \hbox{--} 10) \cdot 10^{9} \,\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$</tex>. We confirm the results by the accord of the quantities obtained from different observations using different methods and by the extrapolation of the photospheric magnetograms into the corona, from which we have obtained a magnetic field strength of about 7 G at that height. Hence, indeed <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta \ge 1$</tex> in the post-eruptive arcade. The high-beta possibility had previously been stated, e.g., by Ichimoto et al. (1994), but still not investigated. We address this issue in terms of the “standard flare model” elaborated by Shibata and Yokoyama. During this event, Yohkoh/SXT observed McKenzie-Hudson dark moving features. Those features are filled with cold material, if they are not empty, and may affect the arcade.

articleTitle: A RIAF Interpretation for the Past Higher Activity of the Galactic Center Black Hole and the 511 keV Annihilation Emission
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: There are several lines of evidence to show that the supermassive black hole at the Galactic center had higher activities in the past than directly observed at present. It is shown here that these lines of evidence can quantitatively and consistently be explained if the mean accretion rate during the past <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 10^7 \,\mathrm{yr}$</tex> has been <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 10^{3\hbox{--}4}$</tex> times higher than the current rate, based on the picture of radiatively inefficient accretion flow (RIAF) and associated outflow that has been successfully applied to Sgr <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{A}^{*}$</tex>. We argue that this increased rate and its duration are theoretically reasonable in the Galactic center environment, while the accretion rate suddenly dropped about 300 yr ago, most likely because of the shell passage of the supernova remnant Sgr A East. The chance probability of witnessing Sgr <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{A}^{*}$</tex> in such a low state is not extremely small (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 0.5\%$</tex>). The outflow energetics is sufficient to keep the hot (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 8 \,\mathrm{keV}$</tex>) diffuse gas observed in the Galactic center region. It is then shown that a significant amount of positrons should have been created around the event horizon during the higher activity phase, and injected into interstellar medium by the outflow. The predicted positron production rate and propagation distance are close to those required to explain the observed 511 keV annihilation line emission from the Galactic bulge, giving a natural explanation for the large bulge-to-disk ratio of the emission. The expected injection energy into interstellar medium is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim \mathrm{MeV}$</tex>, which is also favorable for an explanation of the 511 keV line emission.

articleTitle: The Relative Neighborhood Graph for Estimating Two-Dimensional Voids in the Cold Dark Matter Universe
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: A new technique based on a graph-theoretical approach is proposed for identifying and estimating voids in two-dimensional galaxy distributions. A relative neighborhood graph is utilized for identifying two-dimensional voids. The loop angle that characterizes the size of the voids is defined, and the distribution function as well as the average of loop angles are used for estimating the voids statistically. We applied our new technique to two-dimensional voids in Cold Dark Matter (CDM) simulations. Low-density, middle-density, and high-density CDM models were adopted for examining the nature of two-dimensional voids. From our analyses, we found that the average of the loop angle in the low-density CDM model is apparently larger than that in the middle-density or the high-density CDM models. However, the difference between the middle-density and the high-density CDM models is subtle. We also analyzed the observational two-dimensional galaxy distributions and compared the two-dimensional mock samples that are constructed from CDM simulations. From our analyses, we succeeded to restrict the density parameter of our universe.

articleTitle: Infrared 2–4 Micrometer Spectroscopy and Millimeter Interferometric HCN and HCO+ Observations of the Individual Merging Components of Arp 299
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present ground-based infrared <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K$</tex>–(2–2.5<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\, {\mu \mathrm {m}}$</tex>) and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L$</tex>-band (2.8–4.1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\, {\mu \mathrm {m}}$</tex>) spectroscopy, as well as interferometric observations at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda \sim 3 \,\mathrm{mm}$</tex>, for the individual merging components (A, B, and C) of the luminous infrared galaxy Arp 299. The presence and location of a buried active galactic nucleus (AGN) are investigated. Our sub-arcsec-resolution infrared spectra clearly reveal that the putative buried AGN resides in the nucleus B1 (a subcomponent of B), based on a very low equivalent width of 3.3<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\, {\mu \mathrm {m}}$</tex> polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon emission, a weak 2.3<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\, {\mu \mathrm {m}}$</tex> CO absorption feature, and a large time variation of the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K$</tex>–and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L$</tex>-band continuum fluxes. Our interferometric observations simultaneously obtain HCN (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J = 1 \hbox{--} 0$</tex>) and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{HCO}^{+}$</tex> (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J = 1 \hbox{--} 0$</tex>) emission lines with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 4 {{}^{\prime \prime }}$</tex> resolution, and we find the HCN to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mathrm{HCO}^{+}$</tex> brightness-temperature ratios to be as low as those found in starburst nuclei in all of the major merging components of Arp 299. The low ratio even in the AGN-hosting nucleus B may be due to the presence of a large amount of high-density molecular gas whose chemistry is dominated by coexisting starbursts and/or shocks, rather than by the central strong X-ray-emitting AGN.

articleTitle: Possible Global Magneto-Fluid Structure of the Stellar Convection Zone
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Structures of the magnetic field and velocity in stars are discussed based on the mean field MHD equations. A special case is presented, where the solution is constructed by the Beltrami solution in the stellar convection zone with the symmetry in the azimuthal direction. Magnetic field lines form concentric toroidal magnetic surfaces. The cross-helicity dynamo mechanism induces a mean flow of plasmas. The structure of this driven flow is also shown to constitute toroidal surfaces. Considering the symmetry and the relation of this toroidal magnetic structure with the polarity, it is shown that the latitudinal component of this flow is pole-ward in the northern as well as southern hemispheres. This gives an insight into the role of the magnetic field for the meridional flow.

articleTitle: Chandra and ROSAT Observations of NGC 5044: Profile of Dark Halos in Galaxy Groups
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We combined spatially resolved Chandra data with the ROSAT data to constrain the dark-matter distribution in the galaxy group NGC 5044. Within <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$250 \, h^{-1}_{50} \,\mathrm{kpc}$</tex>, the total mass is found to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 1.6 \times10^{13} \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex>, 12% of which constitutes baryonic mass. Within the inner central regions, the total mass profile exhibits a double structure, typical for groups containing a cD galaxy. Following previous studies of mostly rich galaxy clusters, we studied in detail the nature of such a double structure, whereby we inferred likely interface between the cD galaxy and the surrounding galaxies. For this interesting group, we determined for the first time the galaxy-group interface, which is around 7.5 kpc from the peak of the X-ray emission. The total mass internal to this interface radius is found to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${\sim 7.1 \times10^{10} \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}}$</tex>. Beyond this radius, the total mass profile becomes DM-dominated and the corresponding DM profile is reasonably fitted with the NFW model, yielding results consistent with the observed scatter expected for CDM halos. A power-law fit to the DM mass profile gives <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha = 1.88 \pm 0.32$</tex>, a slope that is within the observed range, but is significantly larger than that of low surface brightness galaxies and self-interacting DM halos.

articleTitle: Pulsar Magnetohydrodynamic Winds
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The acceleration and collimation/decollimation of relativistic magnetocentrifugal winds are discussed concerning a cold plasma from a strongly magnetized, rapidly rotating neutron star in a steady axisymmetric state based on ideal magnetohydrodynamics. There exist unipolar inductors associated with the field line angular frequency, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex>, at the magnetospheric base surface, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$S_{\mathrm{B}}$</tex>, with a huge potential difference between the poles and the equator, which drive electric current through the pulsar magnetosphere. Any “current line” must emanate from one terminal of the unipolar inductor and return to the other, converting the Poynting flux to the kinetic flux of the wind at finite distances. In a plausible field structure satisfying the transfield force-balance equation, the fast surface, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$S_{\mathrm{F}}$</tex>, must exist somewhere between the subasymptotic and asymptotic domains, i.e., at the innermost point along each field line of the asymptotic domain of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\varpi_{\mathrm{A}}^2 / \varpi^2 \ll 1$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\varpi_{\mathrm{A}}$</tex> is the Alfvénic axial distance. The criticality condition at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$S_{\mathrm{F}}$</tex> yields the Lorentz factor, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma_{\mathrm{F}} = \mu_{\varepsilon}^{1/3}$</tex>, and the angular momentum flux, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta$</tex>, as the eigenvalues in terms of the field line angular velocity, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex>, the mass flux per unit flux tube, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\eta$</tex>, and one of the Bernoulli integrals, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu_{\delta}$</tex>, which are assumed to be specifiable as the boundary conditions at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$S_{\mathrm{B}}$</tex>. The other Bernoulli integral, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu_{\varepsilon}$</tex>, is related to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu_{\delta}$</tex> as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu_{\varepsilon} = \mu_{\delta} [1-(\alpha^2 \varpi_{\mathrm{A}}^2 / c^2)]^{-1}$</tex>, and both <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu_{\varepsilon}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\varpi_{\mathrm{A}}^2$</tex> are eigenvalues to be determined by the criticality condition at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$S_{\mathrm{F}}$</tex>. Ongoing MHD acceleration is possible in the superfast domain. This fact may be helpful in resolving a discrepancy between the wind theory and the Crab-nebula model. It is argued that the “anti-collimation theorem” holds for relativistic winds, based on the curvature of field streamlines determined by the transfield force balance. The “theorem” combines with the “current-closure condition” as a global condition in the wind zone to produce a two-component “quasi-conical” field structure as one of the basic properties of MHD outflows of centrifugal origin in the pulsar magnetosphere.

articleTitle: The Virgo High-Resolution CO Survey: VI. Gas Dynamics and Star Formation along the Bar in NGC 4303
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present CO interferometer observations of the barred galaxy NGC 4303 (M 61). This galaxy has a strong gas concentration at the central region and prominent offset ridges at the leading sides of the bar. Sharp velocity gradients are apparent across the ridges. The brightness temperature in the ridges is low, indicating the existence of unresolved molecular clouds. Additionally, an analysis of the newborn stellar clusters revealed in HST images suggests that the parent molecular clouds had masses of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$10^{4-6} \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex>. The observed shear velocity gradient across the ridges is too small to break up giant molecular clouds. Therefore, the clouds are likely to survive passage through the ridges. We discuss a cloud orbit model in a bar potential for understanding the gas distribution, dynamics, and star formation in NGC 4303. The model reproduces the narrow offset ridges and sharp velocity gradients across the ridges, although no shock is associated with the ridges. We discuss cloud–cloud collisions (and close interactions) as a possible triggering mechanism for star formation. The newborn stellar clusters in NGC 4303 are located predominantly at the leading sides of the offset ridges. Cloud orbits are densely populated in the region where the clusters are found, suggesting a high collisional frequency and possibly a high rate of triggered star formation. Cloud-based dynamics is less dissipative than smooth hydrodynamic models, possibly extending the timescales of gas dynamical evolution and gas fueling to central regions in barred galaxies.

articleTitle: Optical Photometrical Observations and Variability for Quasar 4C 29.45
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We reported the result of the long-term optical variability of the blazar 4C 29.45s (QSO 1156+295, Ton 599), carried out by optical photometric observations in the Johnson <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$V$</tex>, Cousins <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$RI$</tex> passbands during 1997 April to 2002 March. We used the 1.56-m telescope of the Shanghai Astronomical Observatory at Sheshan, China, and compiled the post-1974 optical photometric data of the blazar by combining our new observations with the published optical data, and found maximum variations in different passbands: <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Delta U = 4.41 \,\mathrm{mag}, \Delta B = 5.55 \,\mathrm{mag}, \Delta V = 4.53 \,\mathrm{mag}, \Delta R = 5.80 \,\mathrm{mag}$</tex>, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Delta I = 5.34 \,\mathrm{mag}$</tex>. The average color indices are: <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$U-B =-0.54 \pm 0.18 \,\mathrm{mag}, B-V = 0.56 \pm 0.21 \,\mathrm{mag}, B-R = 0.93 \pm 0.18 \,\mathrm{mag}, B-I = 1.51 \pm 0.24 \,\mathrm{mag}, V-R = 0.44 \pm 0.15 \,\mathrm{mag}$</tex>, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$V-I = 1.03 \pm 0.23 \,\mathrm{mag}$</tex>. The post-1974 data give us an excellent opportunity to search for the existence of a possible periodicity in the light curve. In searching for periodicity in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R$</tex> passband light curve, we performed a Jurkevich test and power spectral (Fourier) analysis methods, as well as CLEANest algorithms to remove false signals. We found possible periods of 3.55 and 1.58 years. A possible mechanism for the periodic variability was analyzed.

articleTitle: Soft X-Ray Absorption Due to the Photo-Ionized Plasma in the Low-Mass X-Ray Binary EXO 0748−676 Observed with XMM-Newton Observatory
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We analyzed an effect of the photo-ionization on the continuum spectra using the XMM-Newton archive data of the low-mass X-ray binary EXO 0748-676. We found that the ionization degree of the circumstellar plasma, which modifies the soft X-ray spectrum through absorption, changes largely in association with the X-ray bursts and the dips. The burst light curve below <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 1 \,\mathrm{keV}$</tex> is found to have a major contribution from the persistent emission, which temporary increased during the burst due to a reduction of the opacity of the absorber. We utilized a correlation diagram of the count rates (0.5–1.0 keV vs. 2.0–4.0 keV) to study the effect of photo-ionization during the dips. We found that the correlation can be much better reproduced if we take into account the photo-ionization of the absorber. No partial covering absorption was required, except for the residual flux in the deepest dips.
